explanations.answer: How a mortal can be righteous before God
explanations.explanation: Job takes Bildad's point and turns it into a question: “…how can a mortal be righteous before God?” (Job 9:2). He isn't asking for anything for himself here. He's asking how any person could stand in the right before God. That's a heavy question, friend, and Job asks it plainly.

explanations.answer: How a mortal can win back all he has lost
explanations.explanation: Job doesn't ask about getting anything back in this verse. His question is about being righteous before God (Job 9:2). I know it would be easy to think he's after a refund on his whole life, but that isn't what he asks. Keep your eyes on that word righteous, friend.

explanations.answer: How a mortal can win the respect of his friends
explanations.explanation: This verse isn't about his friends' opinions at all. Job answers Bildad, then asks how a mortal can be righteous before God (Job 9:2). The audience he's worried about is God, not the group chat. Nobody's campaigning for applause here.

explanations.answer: Not once in a thousand times
explanations.explanation: Job says that person “…could not answer Him one time out of a thousand.” (Job 9:3). A thousand tries and not a single good answer. I once had a whole tray where not one cookie held its shape, and even that was a better record than this. Job is showing how far apart a mortal and God stand.

Half would be a pretty strong record, friend, and Job doesn't give anywhere near that. He says the person “…could not answer Him one time out of a thousand.” (Job 9:3). Job's number is one in a thousand, and he says even that one isn't there.

explanations.answer: Only on the very first try
explanations.explanation: No beginner's luck in this courtroom. Job says the person “…could not answer Him one time out of a thousand.” (Job 9:3). That means not on the first try, and not on any try after it.

Job just called God “mighty in strength” (Job 9:4), and then he piles up the proof. Mountains move, the earth shakes and the sun is commanded not to shine (Job 9:5-7). Every item on that list is something only God could do. That's what Job wants you to see about Him.

explanations.answer: How gently He tends the earth
explanations.explanation: Look at the verbs on that list, friend. God moves mountains, shakes the earth from its place and seals off the stars (Job 9:5-7). Job even says He overturns mountains “in His anger” (Job 9:5). This list is about power, not gentleness.

explanations.answer: How He rests after His work
explanations.explanation: Job never mentions resting in these verses. He keeps listing what God does: He moves, shakes, commands, seals, stretches and treads (Job 9:5-8). Nothing on the list slows down. Job is showing power, and the power keeps going.

explanations.answer: He would still dread all his sufferings
explanations.explanation: Job says, “I would still dread all my sufferings; I know that You will not acquit me.” (Job 9:28). Putting on a smile wouldn't change what he's carrying. A smile on the outside is just a smile, friend. Job says the dread stays.

explanations.answer: His friends would still walk away from him
explanations.explanation: His friends aren't in this verse. Job says, “I would still dread all my sufferings; I know that You will not acquit me.” (Job 9:28). The thing that stays is his dread. It's about what he's feeling inside.

explanations.answer: His pain would slowly fade on its own
explanations.explanation: Job says the opposite. He says, “I would still dread all my sufferings…” (Job 9:28). Faking a smile doesn't make it go away in his picture. The dread stays right where it is.

Job says it wouldn't work. He says, “If I should wash myself with snow and cleanse my hands with lye, then You would plunge me into the pit, and even my own clothes would despise me.” (Job 9:30-31). So the scrubbing doesn't get him clean in his picture. That's how hopeless he feels.

A stranger isn't what Job is missing. He says, “Nor is there a mediator between us, to lay his hand upon us both.” (Job 9:33). A mediator would stand between Job and God. Job says nobody's there.

That's right. Job says, “Then I would speak without fear of Him. But as it is, I am on my own.” (Job 9:35). The “then” is for after God's rod is removed. For now, he says he's on his own.

Job says, “I will say to God: Do not condemn me! Let me know why You prosecute me.” (Job 10:2). He wants a reason. I think anybody in pain would ask the same thing, friend. He asks it straight to God.

explanations.answer: How long he has left to live
explanations.explanation: Job isn't asking for a number of days here. He says, “Let me know why You prosecute me.” (Job 10:2). What he's after is the reason. That's the question on his heart.

Job asks if God's days are like a man's, “that You should seek my iniquity and search out my sin” (Job 10:6). So this is what Job says God is doing to him. It's how Job sees it. Job is asking God to look at that.

Job doesn't say anything about forgotten good deeds here. He says God seeks his iniquity and searches out his sin (Job 10:6). It's the searching that he's talking about. Good deeds don't come up in this verse.

Job says it right in his question to God: “…though You know that I am not guilty, and there is no deliverance from Your hand?” (Job 10:7). So Job says God knows he isn't guilty. He says it alongside his fear that there's no way out.
